subject: math
title: Grade 3 Area
seo_title: Grade 3 Area Worksheets: Free Math with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Use square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²) to estimate, measure, and compare the areas of various two-dimensional shapes, including those with curved sides
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 area worksheets for the Ontario math curriculum (E2.7, E2.8, E2.9): compare areas by covering, count square units and half squares, avoid gaps and overlaps, use cm² and m², and estimate curved shapes on a grid. 100 questions with an answer key, great EQAO practice.
key_big: Area is the space a shape covers. Cover it with same-size squares, with no gaps and no overlaps, and count them.
key_sub: Two half squares make one square. Use cm² for small things and m² for big spaces. For curved shapes, count squares that are half or more covered.
body_html:
What is area?

Area is the amount of space a flat shape covers. We measure it by covering the shape with units that are all the same size, and counting them.

The size of the unit matters. Small units: you need more of them. Big units: you need fewer. To compare two areas, use the same unit.

No gaps and no overlaps

Units must cover the whole shape, with no gaps, no overlaps and nothing hanging over the edge.

Count square units

Squares are the best units: they fit together with no gaps. Count the squares inside, row by row.

Example

A rectangle has 3 rows of 5 squares. What is its area?

Skip count by the row: 5, 10, 15.

Answer: 15 square units

Two half squares make one whole square.

Square centimetres and square metres

A square centimetre (1 cm²) is a square 1 cm on each side, about the size of a fingernail. Use cm² for small things such as a stamp or a page.

A square metre (1 m²) is a square 1 m on each side. Use m² for big spaces such as a floor, a garden or a rink.

MeasuringSmall thingsBig things
Length (cm, m)cm: a pencil, a photom: a hallway, a hockey rink
Area (cm², m²)cm²: a stamp, a sticky notem²: a classroom floor, a garden

Estimate the area of a curved shape

Curved shapes do not fit the squares exactly, so we estimate. Count each whole square. Count a square as 1 if half or more is covered. Leave out squares that are less than half covered.

Example

A garden is marked into 1 m squares: 4 rows of 5. What is its area?

4 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20. Each square is 1 m².

Answer: 20 m²

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting the sides around the edgeThat is the perimeter. For area, count the squares inside
Counting only the squares along the edgeCount every square, the inside ones too
Leaving gaps or overlapping unitsCover with no gaps and no overlaps
Comparing counts of different-size unitsUse the same unit for both shapes
Counting a half square as a whole oneTwo half squares make one square
Writing cm or m for an areaArea is in square units: cm² or m²

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about area in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: They measure area by covering shapes with same-size units with no gaps or overlaps, see that smaller units mean a bigger count, and use square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²) to estimate, measure and compare areas, including shapes with curved sides.

faq.q: What is the difference between area and perimeter?
faq.a: Area is the space inside a shape, measured in square units such as cm² or m². Perimeter is the distance around the outside, measured in cm or m.

faq.q: Why do gaps and overlaps matter when measuring area?
faq.a: Gaps leave space uncounted, so the area comes out too small. Overlaps and units hanging over the edge count space twice or outside the shape, so the area comes out too big.

faq.q: Is area on the Grade 3 EQAO math assessment?
faq.a: The Grade 3 EQAO math assessment is based on the Ontario curriculum, and measurement, including area, is part of it. Counting square units and choosing cm² or m² are good skills to practise.

items.q: Jayden and Hana cover the same table. Jayden uses 8 big cards. Hana uses 24 small sticky notes. Why are the numbers different?
items.e: It is the same table, so the area is the same. Smaller units are needed in bigger numbers.

items.q: Chloe covers a bulletin board with sheets of paper, with no gaps or overlaps. There are 4 rows of 5. What is the area in sheets of paper?
items.e: Count by rows: 4 rows of 5 is 5, 10, 15, 20. The area is 20 sheets of paper. (4 + 5 = 9 only adds the rows and the columns.)

items.q: Each shape is covered by square units. Which shape has the largest area?
items.e: Count the squares that cover each shape: A 5, B 9, C 8, D 7. Shape B covers the most squares, so it has the largest area.

items.q: A red trapezoid pattern block covers the same space as 3 green triangles. Which covers more space: 2 trapezoids or 5 triangles?
items.e: Change the trapezoids into triangles: 2 trapezoids = 3 + 3 = 6 triangles. 6 is more than 5. Compare areas in the same unit.

items.q: This triangle is covered by green triangle pattern blocks. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Count every triangle, the ones pointing up and the ones pointing down: 3 up + 1 down = 4 triangles.

items.q: This hexagon is covered by green triangle pattern blocks. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Count every triangle, the ones pointing up and the ones pointing down: 3 up + 3 down = 6 triangles.

items.q: Each shape is covered by square units. Which shape has the largest area?
items.e: Count the squares that cover each shape: A 5, B 8, C 9, D 7. Shape C covers the most squares, so it has the largest area.

items.q: This triangle is covered by green triangle pattern blocks. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Count every triangle, the ones pointing up and the ones pointing down: 6 up + 3 down = 9 triangles.

items.q: Benjamin covers shape A with 6 big tiles. Owen covers shape B with 6 small tiles. Which is true?
c: Each has an area of 6 cm²
items.e: Both counts are 6, but the units are different sizes. 6 big tiles cover more space than 6 small tiles. To compare areas, use the same unit.

items.q: Which unit would you need the fewest of to cover the gym floor?
items.e: The bigger the unit, the fewer you need. Floor mats are the biggest units here.

items.q: This trapezoid is covered by green triangle pattern blocks. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Count every triangle, the ones pointing up and the ones pointing down: 4 up + 3 down = 7 triangles.

items.q: This trapezoid is covered by green triangle pattern blocks. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Count every triangle, the ones pointing up and the ones pointing down: 3 up + 2 down = 5 triangles.

items.q: A blue rhombus pattern block is covered by 2 green triangles. A shape is covered by 4 blue rhombuses. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Each rhombus is 2 triangles. 4 rhombuses: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 triangles.

items.q: Each shape is covered by square units. Which shape has the smallest area?
items.e: Count the squares that cover each shape: A 7, B 8, C 6, D 5. Shape D covers the fewest squares, so it has the smallest area.

items.q: Olivia covers a desk with index cards, with no gaps or overlaps. There are 3 rows of 6. What is the area in index cards?
items.e: Count by rows: 3 rows of 6 is 6, 12, 18. The area is 18 index cards. (3 + 6 = 9 only adds the rows and the columns.)

items.q: A yellow hexagon pattern block is covered exactly by 6 green triangles. How many green triangles cover 2 hexagons?
items.e: Each hexagon is 6 triangles. 2 hexagons: 6 + 6 = 12 triangles. (6 + 2 = 8 adds the number of hexagons instead.)

items.q: Nathan covers a placemat with sticky notes, with no gaps or overlaps. There are 3 rows of 5. What is the area in sticky notes?
items.e: Count by rows: 3 rows of 5 is 5, 10, 15. The area is 15 sticky notes. (3 + 5 = 8 only adds the rows and the columns.)

items.q: Leah covers a rug with large square tiles and needs 10. How many tiles will she need if she uses smaller tiles?
items.e: The rug does not change. Smaller tiles each cover less, so more of them are needed.

items.q: Which unit would you need the most of to cover a desk?
items.e: The smaller the unit, the more of them you need. Sticky notes are the smallest here.

items.q: This parallelogram is covered by green triangle pattern blocks. What is its area in triangles?
items.e: Count every triangle, the ones pointing up and the ones pointing down: 4 up + 4 down = 8 triangles.

sets.title: Count square units and half squares

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 14. The area is 14 cm². Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 20).

items.q: What is the area of the shaded house shape? Two half squares make one whole square.
items.e: There are 14 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 whole squares. 14 + 2 = 16 square units.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 2 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 13. The area is 13 square units. Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 18).

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 12. The area is 12 cm². Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 16).

items.q: A shape on a grid covers 11 whole squares and 2 half squares. What is its area in square units?
items.e: Two half squares make one whole square, so 2 half squares make 1. 11 + 1 = 12 square units.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside, row by row: 4 rows of 3 is 3, 6, 9, 12. The area is 12 square units. (14 is the number of sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 5 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 21. The area is 21 square units. Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 26).

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside, row by row: 2 rows of 5 is 5, 10. The area is 10 square units. (14 is the number of sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded triangle? Two half squares make one whole square.
items.e: There are 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 whole squares. 6 + 2 = 8 square units.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. The area is 7 square units. Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 12).

items.q: A shape on a grid covers 6 whole squares and 6 half squares. What is its area in square units?
items.e: Two half squares make one whole square, so 6 half squares make 3. 6 + 3 = 9 square units.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 10. The area is 10 square units. Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 14).

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: There are 19 whole squares and 1 half square. 1 half square is ½ of a square. 19 + ½ = 19½ cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: There are 15 whole squares and 1 half square. 1 half square is ½ of a square. 15 + ½ = 15½ cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded diamond shape?
items.e: There are 4 whole squares and 8 half squares. 8 halves make 4 whole squares. 4 + 4 = 8 cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside, row by row: 2 rows of 6 is 6, 12. The area is 12 cm². (16 is the number of sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded trapezoid? Two half squares make one whole square.
items.e: There are 12 whole squares and 3 half squares. 3 halves make 1½ whole squares. 12 + 1½ = 13½ square units.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: 6 + 6 + 6 + 3 = 21. The area is 21 cm². Count each square once, not the sides around the edge (that would be the perimeter, 20).

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside, row by row: 5 rows of 4 is 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. The area is 20 cm². (18 is the number of sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: A shape on a grid covers 8 whole squares and 4 half squares. What is its area in square units?
items.e: Two half squares make one whole square, so 4 half squares make 2. 8 + 2 = 10 square units.

items.q: Mei covers a book with index cards, but the cards overlap. She counts 14 cards. What is the real area of the book?
items.e: Where cards overlap, the same space is counted twice. So the real area is less than 14 cards.

items.q: Why are square tiles better than round counters for measuring area?
items.e: Round counters cannot fit together without gaps, so some space is not counted. Squares fit together with no gaps and no overlaps.

items.q: Square tiles are placed along the top row and down one side. How many tiles will cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 6 tiles fit across. The side shows there are 3 rows. 3 rows of 6: 6, 12, 18. The rectangle needs 18 tiles.

items.q: Which rule helps you measure area correctly?
items.e: Cover the whole shape with units of the same size, with no gaps and no overlaps.

items.q: Each picture shows square tiles on a tray. Which picture has tiles that overlap?
items.e: A has gaps between the tiles. B has tiles hanging over the edge. C has tiles that overlap. D has no gaps and no overlaps. So the answer is C.

items.q: Some tiles are missing from this tray. What is the area of the tray in square tiles?
items.e: The area is the whole tray, gaps too. 4 rows of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, so 24 tiles. Counting only the tiles you see (21) leaves out the gaps.

items.q: Square tiles are placed along the top row and down one side. How many tiles will cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 5 tiles fit across. The side shows there are 4 rows. 4 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20. The rectangle needs 20 tiles.

items.q: Each picture shows square tiles on a tray. Which picture has gaps between the tiles?
items.e: A has no gaps and no overlaps. B has gaps between the tiles. C has tiles hanging over the edge. D has tiles that overlap. So the answer is B.

items.q: Liam is covering a tray with square tiles. How many more tiles does he need so there are no gaps?
items.e: Count the empty spaces, including the ones at the edge: 4. (12 tiles are already down, and 16 is the total.)

items.q: Square tiles are placed along the top row and down one side. How many tiles will cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 6 tiles fit across. The side shows there are 4 rows. 4 rows of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. The rectangle needs 24 tiles.

items.q: Lucas lets some tiles hang over the edge of a tray. What happens to his count?
items.e: Parts of the tiles are outside the tray, but they are counted anyway. So the count is bigger than the real area.

items.q: Each picture shows square tiles on a tray. Which picture shows the right way to measure the area of the tray?
items.e: A has gaps between the tiles. B has tiles that overlap. C has no gaps and no overlaps. D has tiles hanging over the edge. Tiles must fit inside the edge with no gaps and no overlaps, as in C.

items.q: Some tiles are missing from this tray. What is the area of the tray in square tiles?
items.e: The area is the whole tray, gaps too. 4 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, so 20 tiles. Counting only the tiles you see (17) leaves out the gaps.

items.q: Square tiles are placed along the top row and down one side. How many tiles will cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 5 tiles fit across. The side shows there are 3 rows. 3 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15. The rectangle needs 15 tiles.

items.q: Square tiles are placed along the top row and down one side. How many tiles will cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 4 tiles fit across. The side shows there are 4 rows. 4 rows of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16. The rectangle needs 16 tiles.

items.q: Square tiles are placed along the top row and down one side. How many tiles will cover the whole rectangle?
items.e: The top row shows 4 tiles fit across. The side shows there are 3 rows. 3 rows of 4: 4, 8, 12. The rectangle needs 12 tiles.

items.q: Ava is covering a tray with square tiles. How many more tiles does she need so there are no gaps?
items.e: Count the empty spaces, including the ones at the edge: 5. (13 tiles are already down, and 18 is the total.)

items.q: Ethan counts 18 square tiles on a mat. Aiden covers the same mat with the same tiles and counts 24, with no gaps or overlaps. What did Ethan do wrong?
items.e: Ethan got fewer tiles than the correct count. Gaps make a count too small. (Overlaps would make it too big.)

items.q: Arjun is covering a tray with square tiles. How many more tiles does he need so there are no gaps?
items.e: Count the empty spaces, including the ones at the edge: 3. (12 tiles are already down, and 15 is the total.)

items.q: Maya covers her desk with sticky notes but leaves gaps between them. She counts 20 sticky notes. What is the real area of the desk?
items.e: The gaps are part of the desk too, but no sticky notes were counted there. So the real area is more than 20 sticky notes.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the squares, row by row: 3 + 5 = 8. Each square is 1 cm², so the area is 8 cm². Area uses square units: cm², not cm.

items.q: This is a plan of a school garden. Each square is 1 m². What is its area?
items.e: Count the squares: 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 13. Each square is 1 m², so the area is 13 m².

items.q: About how big is the cover of a notebook?
items.e: A notebook is about 28 cm by 21 cm, so about 600 squares of 1 cm² cover it. 60 m² would be a whole classroom, and cm is for length, not area.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a classroom floor?
items.e: A floor is big and we cover the space inside it, so use square metres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: This is a plan of a classroom reading corner. Each square is 1 m². What is its area?
items.e: Count the squares: 6 + 6 + 6 + 1 = 19. Each square is 1 m², so the area is 19 m².

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a postage stamp?
items.e: A stamp is small and we cover the space inside it, so use square centimetres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: About how big is the floor of a classroom?
items.e: A classroom is about 8 m by 8 m: 8 rows of 8 one-metre squares is 64, so about 60 m². 6 m² is a small rug. A floor needs square metres, not square centimetres.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the distance around a photo?
items.e: The distance around is a length (the perimeter), not an area. A photo is small, so use centimetres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded arrow shape?
items.e: There are 8 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 whole squares. 8 + 2 = 10 cm².

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the length of the school hallway?
items.e: This is a length, not an area. A hallway is long, so use metres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Which area is the biggest?
items.e: A square metre is much bigger than a square centimetre: a 1 m² square holds far more than 300 squares of 1 cm². So 3 m² is the biggest.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of an outdoor skating rink?
items.e: A rink is big and area is the space inside, so use square metres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded tree shape?
items.e: There are 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 whole squares. 6 + 2 = 8 cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the squares, row by row: 4 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 9. Each square is 1 cm², so the area is 9 cm². Area uses square units: cm², not cm.

items.q: Which has an area of about 1 cm²?
items.e: 1 cm² is a square 1 cm long and 1 cm wide, about the size of the nail on your little finger.

items.q: About how big is a square sticky note?
items.e: A sticky note is about 8 cm by 8 cm: 8 rows of 8 is 64, so about 60 cm².

items.q: Which is bigger: 5 m² or 50 cm²?
items.e: 1 m² is a square 1 m (100 cm) on each side. Even one m² is far bigger than 50 squares of 1 cm². Look at the unit, not only the number.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded sailboat shape?
items.e: There are 5 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 whole squares. 5 + 2 = 7 cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the squares, row by row: 5 + 5 + 1 = 11. Each square is 1 cm², so the area is 11 cm². Area uses square units: cm², not cm.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of the front of a cereal box?
items.e: A cereal box is small and area is the space inside, so use square centimetres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: On a snow day, the class marks out a square area for a snow fort, 5 m by 5 m, in 1 m squares. What is its area?
items.e: 5 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. The area is 25 m². (20 m is the distance around.)

items.q: You estimate the area of a curved shape on a grid. Which squares do you count?
c: Whole and half or more covered
items.e: Count every whole square, and count a square as 1 if half or more of it is covered. Leave out squares that are less than half covered. The bits you count and leave out roughly balance.

items.q: This is a plan of a patio. Each square is 1 m². How many 1 m² patio stones cover it with no gaps?
items.e: Count the squares, row by row: 4 + 4 + 4 + 6 = 18. One stone covers each square, so 18 stones are needed. (24 counts the empty squares in the corner too.)
Whole squares: 9. Squares half or more covered: 7. Estimate: 9 + 7 = 16 m². Squares less than half covered (13) are not counted.

items.q: A hallway rug covers 8 m². A bedroom rug covers 6 m². What area do the two rugs cover together?
items.e: Add the areas: 8 + 6 = 14 m². Area is in square metres, so the answer is 14 m², not 14 m.

items.q: A floor needs 4 rows of 5 square tiles. 13 tiles are already down. How many more tiles are needed?
items.e: Whole floor: 4 rows of 5 is 5, 10, 15, 20 tiles. Still needed: 20 − 13 = 7 tiles.

items.q: The teacher has 30 carpet tiles. The carpet for circle time needs 5 rows of 5 tiles. How many tiles are left over?
items.e: Carpet: 5 rows of 5 is 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 tiles. Left over: 30 − 25 = 5 tiles.

items.q: For Thanksgiving, Mateo covers a paper placemat with square stickers: 3 rows of 7 stickers, with no gaps. What is the area of the placemat in stickers?
items.e: 3 rows of 7: 7, 14, 21 stickers. (16 is only the stickers around the edge, and 14 is 2 rows.)

items.q: The reading corner floor is covered with square carpet tiles. Each tile is 1 m². There are 4 rows of 6 tiles. What is the area of the reading corner?
items.e: Each tile is 1 m², so count the tiles: 4 rows of 6 is 6, 12, 18, 24. The area is 24 m².

items.q: Amira wants to know how much carpet will cover her bedroom floor. What should she find?
items.e: Covering a floor is area: the space inside. A floor is big, so the area is in square metres (m²).
Whole squares: 7. Squares half or more covered: 8. Estimate: 7 + 8 = 15 cm². Squares less than half covered (10) are not counted.

items.q: Kai’s garden is 4 rows of 3 squares. Jayden’s garden is 2 rows of 5 squares. Each square is 1 m². Whose garden has the bigger area?
items.e: Kai: 4 rows of 3 is 12 m². Jayden: 2 rows of 5 is 10 m². 12 − 10 = 2, so Kai’s garden is bigger by 2 m². (4 + 3 and 2 + 5 are both 7, but that is not the area. A longer row does not mean a bigger area.)

items.q: In a school garden, tomatoes fill 6 squares, beans fill 4 squares and carrots fill 5 squares. Each square is 1 m². What area is planted?
items.e: Add the squares: 6 + 4 + 5 = 15. Each square is 1 m², so 15 m² is planted.

items.q: Each gym mat covers 2 m². The class lays 6 mats on the floor with no gaps or overlaps. What area do the mats cover?
items.e: 6 mats of 2 m² each: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. They cover 12 m². (6 + 2 = 8 adds instead.)

items.q: Zoe’s garden covers 12 squares of 1 m². Noah’s garden covers 9 squares of 1 m². How much bigger is Zoe’s garden?
items.e: Find the difference: 12 − 9 = 3. Zoe’s garden is 3 m² bigger. (21 m² is both gardens together.)
Whole squares: 5. Squares half or more covered: 8. Estimate: 5 + 8 = 13 cm². Squares less than half covered (10) are not counted.

items.q: Emma’s family plants a vegetable garden. It is marked into 1 m squares: 3 rows of 5 squares. What is the area of the garden?
items.e: 3 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15. Each square is 1 m², so the area is 15 m². (16 is the distance around, in m.)
Whole squares: 6. Squares half or more covered: 5. Estimate: 6 + 5 = 11 m². Squares less than half covered (11) are not counted.
Whole squares: 8. Squares half or more covered: 5. Estimate: 8 + 5 = 13 cm². Squares less than half covered (12) are not counted.
Whole squares: 8. Squares half or more covered: 5. Estimate: 8 + 5 = 13 cm². Squares less than half covered (15) are not counted.
